interactions.hypothesis: An error in one conference offset moves legs in opposite directions when the backed sides sit on opposite sides of it (Big Ten beating SEC versus Big 12 beating Big Ten), and in the same direction when they sit on the same side; pair dependence takes either sign.
Underdog-cover-and-under dependence is strongest when the expected margin sits near the spread strike and weak for large mismatches.
Opt-outs add leg-specific strength loss with wide uncertainty; in postseason packs this inflates posterior spread per leg and the joint tail.

In the sampled 3- and 4-leg packs the legs load on different conferences: Indiana over Alabama backs Big Ten against SEC, Texas Tech over Oregon backs Big 12 against Big Ten, Georgia over Ole Miss is intra-SEC, and in the 4-leg pack Ohio St. over Miami (FL) backs Big Ten against ACC, on the same side as Indiana. An offset error therefore pushes opposed legs in opposite directions (negative dependence: the all-hit probability is below the product of the leg probabilities whatever the sign of the realised error) and same-side legs together; the sign follows the signed exposure.
interactions.how_to_test: Back-test postseason slates: compare realised all-leg hit rates of same-side, opposed-side and intra-conference leg pairs against product-of-marginal forecasts, separately by sign of exposure product.

interactions.hypothesis: With few expected possessions, scoring variance shrinks for both margin and total, so an underdog +7.5 and under 48.5 become strongly positively dependent; with many possessions the margin variance grows while the under is unlikely, and the dependence weakens.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the joint-to-product ratio of (dog cover, under) by expected-possessions tercile on historical games.

interactions.hypothesis: For favourite-cover-plus-over combinations, the joint grows with the strength gap until the favourite's lead triggers starter removal; beyond that point the total stalls while margin is capped, so the joint flattens.
interactions.how_to_test: Plot P(fav cover and over) against expected margin and fit a change-point near the starter-pull lead size.

interactions.hypothesis: Losing a starting QB or several draft-bound starters reduces leg win probability proportionally; because the pack multiplies legs, the pack price falls by the same factor, and simultaneous news on two legs compounds.
interactions.how_to_test: In finalized postseason packs, compare predicted pack probabilities using pregame-confirmed versus season-default starters against settlement.

interactions.hypothesis: Long postseason layoffs (three to five weeks) add uncertainty to team strength that is absent in the regular season, so posterior spread per leg widens and the pack's distribution moves toward the extremes in postseason regimes.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare residual variance of postseason versus regular-season games for teams with 21+ day layoffs.

nonlinearities.shape: sigmoid per leg, multiplied across legs
nonlinearities.why: Pack probability is a product of sigmoids in rating gaps; a one-point error in the weakest leg's gap moves the pack more than the same error in a heavy-favourite leg because that leg's sigmoid slope is steepest near even odds.

nonlinearities.shape: lumpy at key numbers 3 and 7 around the +7.5 strike
nonlinearities.why: Final margins cluster at exactly 7 and 3, so moving the spread strike from 6.5 to 7.5 changes the cover leg by a jump, and the joint with the total inherits that step.

mechanism_review.summary: A pre-pack is a conjunction. For moneyline packs, the outcome is the product of each named team winning, adjusted for dependence: game noise is independent across games, but the estimate of every leg uses the same rating model, and postseason slates feature cross-conference games where conference offsets are poorly identified, so model error is shared with a sign set by each leg's conference exposure (opposed legs are negatively dependent); opt-out waves before bowls add slate shocks. For the same-game pack, the spread and total legs come from one bivariate score distribution where pace, script and blowout truncation tie margin to total. Leg probabilities multiply, so a small bias in each compounds across three or four legs, and the conjunction is most sensitive to the least likely leg. Contract mechanics add a layer: legs settle at different times and the void handling for a moved game is not stated.

stages.name: Per-leg game winner or cover probability
stages.description: For each named game, non-market ratings, opponent-adjusted efficiency, confirmed quarterback, venue (campus CFP first round versus neutral later rounds) and postseason layoff give the probability that the named team wins or covers. Because CFB games always produce a winner through overtime, moneyline legs have no tie branch, which simplifies each leg to a single Bernoulli.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli per leg; win probability is a sigmoid in rating gap with fat margin tails in mismatches.

stages.name: Cross-game dependence of legs
stages.description: Leg outcomes in different games share the rating model's errors. In bowl and CFP slates, teams from two or three power conferences meet each other after a season with few cross-conference games, so conference offsets are uncertain. Each leg loads on the offsets with a signed exposure: +1 for the backed team's conference, -1 for the opponent's, 0 if both share one. In the sampled 4-leg pack Indiana over Alabama loads +Big Ten/-SEC, Texas Tech over Oregon loads +Big 12/-Big Ten Ohio St. over Miami (FL) loads +Big Ten/-ACC and Georgia over Ole Miss loads nothing, so a Big Ten error moves the Indiana and Ohio St. legs together and the Texas Tech leg against them. Opt-out waves add common shocks; weather is kept within-game.
stages.distribution: Pairwise correlation is signed by conference exposure (positive for same-side legs, negative for opposed legs, near zero for intra-conference legs), small in size; joint tails differ from independence in a direction set by the pack composition.

stages.name: Within-game margin-total joint for same-game packs
stages.description: For a spread-plus-total pack, possessions, efficiency and score state jointly produce margin and total. Low-possession, low-efficiency games compress margins (helping the underdog +7.5) and stay under; blowouts push margin and total up together until starters are pulled. The joint pmf at the half-point strikes, with key-number lumps near 7 and 3, is what pays.
stages.distribution: Bivariate lattice pmf of (margin, total) with correlation sign depending on the favoured side; key-number spikes.

stages.name: Conjunction, timing and settlement
stages.description: The pack pays one dollar only if all legs hit. Legs in multi-date packs resolve sequentially, and the sampled rules carry no void or overtime wording for spread and total legs, so the treatment of a moved or cancelled leg game and of overtime points is unknown. Overtime itself guarantees moneyline legs a winner under the college format.
stages.distribution: Product (with dependence) of Bernoulli legs; sensitivity of the pack to leg i equals the joint probability of the other legs.

season_stat_leader.label: CFB season stat leader
contract_types: College Football Big Ten Stats Leaders
season_stat_leader.target: Probability that a named player finishes the regular season as the leader of a stated counting stat (rushing yards, receiving yards, passing touchdowns, sacks) in a conference or in Division I, with ties paying $1/N.
season_stat_leader.mechanism: A leader market is an order statistic: each eligible player's end-of-regular-season total equals the current total plus remaining production, and YES requires the named player's total to be the maximum. Remaining production is games remaining (byes, Hawaii exemption, cancellations; conference title games excluded) times participation times volume share of team plays times efficiency against remaining opponents, with overdispersed game-to-game variation. Teammates compete for the same carries or targets; QB health links receivers to passers; sacks depend on opponents' dropbacks. Late in the season the current gap dominates; early, usage and health do. Ties pay $1/N, which matters for small-integer stats. The season_outcome blueprint inputs (standings, playoff format, polls, futures coherence, market ratings) were not carried over: they describe team outcomes, and the inputs here are player-volume inputs for an order statistic.

inputs.why: Observed state only: current regular-season totals, gap to rivals and games remaining per team; its bundled projection is discarded in favour of the field simulation.
Order-statistic simulation over the whole field including unlisted players and teammates competing for usage.
Carry, target and snap shares decide how much of the team's volume each rushing or receiving candidate gets.
Pass-rush snaps and sack rate per snap drive the SEC sacks race; offence inputs say nothing about it.
Per-game injury and miss probability by position; a missed game removes a full game of production and the rules void to NO if the player never plays. Job-loss risk is handled by a separate input.
Team rush attempts given expected script set the volume pool for a rushing-yards leader.
Team dropbacks given script set volume for passing-TD and receiving-yards leaders.
Sacks need opponent dropbacks; facing pass-heavy opponents raises a pass rusher's sack chances.
Touchdowns per scoring trip and the pass/rush split decide passing TD accumulation for a QB.
Yards per carry and explosive-run rate scale rushing-yards accumulation per opportunity.
Remaining opponents' allowed rushing, receiving and sack rates adjust per-game projections.
Stars on dominant teams sit in fourth quarters of blowouts, cutting volume despite strong teams.
A receiving or passing leader depends on the starting QB staying healthy; a backup lowers passing production.
Overdispersed game-level production and long-run tails decide how fast a trailing candidate can catch up.
Tie probability at the top for discrete stats determines the $1/N payout share.
Late-season redshirt or draft-related sit-outs remove remaining regular-season games.
November wind and snow suppress passing and favour rushing volume in remaining outdoor games.
Regular-season scope, conference-title-game exclusion, play-in-conference requirement and $1/N tie payout come from the rules.
Stat corrections and definitions (college sacks counted as rushing losses, half sacks) differ between providers and the official record.
PPA per dropback and sack rate of the passing unit scale yards per target and passing-TD conversion.
Remaining-opponent strength adjusts expected per-game production over the final weeks.
Opponent pass-protection sack rates adjust a rusher's sack chance in each remaining game.
Absent teammates vacate carries and targets, re-allocating usage to a candidate.
Run/pass identity and coordinator changes set how much a feature back or pass rusher is used.
Team plays per game set the opportunity pool for carries, targets and dropbacks.
Depth position and OR designations reveal role and teammate competition for carries or targets.
Eliminated teams and bowl-eligibility stakes affect late-season sit-outs and usage.
Settled leader and tie outcome of prior seasons checks the order-statistic and 1/N payout logic.
Keeps the race field from treating a named incumbent QB or back as certain to keep the job for the full regular season; relevant to every series, most to passing TDs.

interactions.hypothesis: A missed game costs the leader more when the gap to second place is smaller than one game's expected production.
Stars on dominant teams get high per-game share but lose fourth-quarter snaps, so strong team quality helps volume up to a point and then hurts it.
Sack accumulation scales with the product of pass-rush rate and opponent dropbacks; a rusher facing run-heavy opponents loses ground.

One missed game costs a player about one game of expected production. If the leader's cushion exceeds that, a single absence rarely flips the race; if it is below, a missed game hands the lead over. The effect of injury risk on price therefore jumps around a gap of one game's production.
interactions.how_to_test: In the field simulation, vary the leader's per-game miss probability and plot P(leader) against gap measured in games of production.

interactions.hypothesis: Better teams run more plays and score more, raising a feature back's volume, but in blowouts the starter sits for the fourth quarter. Expected season carries rise with team strength and then flatten or fall for heavy favourites, favouring leaders on good-not-dominant teams.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress per-game carries of top-3 RBs on pregame expected margin with a quadratic term, FBS 2014+.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected sacks per game equal pass-rush snaps (driven by opponent dropbacks) times sacks per snap; a top rusher facing two run-heavy service-academy-style opponents gains less than a weaker rusher facing pass-heavy teams.
interactions.how_to_test: Model per-game sacks as Poisson with log-link on log(opponent dropbacks) and rusher rate; test the offset coefficient near 1.

interactions.hypothesis: A receiving-yards leader's projection is conditional on his QB: if the starter is lost, team pass yards fall and target concentration may change, so the leader's probability collapses while a rival on a stable team gains.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare receiver per-game yards before and after starting-QB changes, 2014+, controlling for opponent.

interactions.hypothesis: For passing TDs and sacks the top of the leaderboard is often bunched within one or two units; the 1/N payout then makes a near-leader's value much higher than P(sole leader) alone, especially with two candidates on a 0.5-sack lattice.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare simulated sole-leader probability versus expected payout including ties by stat type; check historical tie frequencies match.

nonlinearities.shape: sigmoid in gap divided by remaining-production SD
nonlinearities.why: P(lead holds) depends on the standardized gap; with few games left the SD shrinks, so the same yardage gap becomes nearly decisive late but is soft in October.

nonlinearities.shape: step losses of one game of production; absorbing at season-ending injury
nonlinearities.why: Availability does not shade production smoothly: each missed game removes a whole game of volume, and a season-ending injury freezes the total, so its effect on probability is discontinuous.

nonlinearities.shape: lattice spikes for integer and half-integer stats
nonlinearities.why: Passing TDs move in units and sacks in halves, so probability mass concentrates on ties in a way that has no analogue for yards.

mechanism_review.summary: The leader is the maximum of many players' season totals, so the named player's probability depends on his current total, the field's totals, and the distribution of everyone's remaining production. Remaining production is a product: regular-season games left (schedule, byes, cancellations; title games excluded) times probability of playing each game times opportunity volume (team plays times usage share for backs and receivers, dropbacks and red-zone trips for passing TDs, opponent dropbacks times pass-rush snaps for sacks) times per-opportunity efficiency against the remaining opponents, with fourth-quarter volume lost in blowouts. Game-level production is overdispersed (long runs, multi-sack games), teammates share volume, and players on one team share pace and QB shocks. With a few weeks left the race is mostly the current gap plus injury risk; the 1/N tie rule adds value for discrete stats.

stages.name: Current leaderboard and games remaining
stages.description: As of the query week, each contender has a regular-season total and a count of remaining regular-season games, which differs by team because byes fall in different weeks, a Hawaii road trip allows a 13th game and cancelled games are not replaced; conference title games do not count. The gap to the leader measured in expected games of production is the main state variable in November.
stages.distribution: Deterministic current totals; games remaining is a small integer (0-5 in November) per team.

stages.name: Participation and health
stages.description: Each remaining game requires the player to be available. Running backs and edge rushers carry higher per-game injury risk than quarterbacks; draft prospects on eliminated teams sometimes sit late games, and a never-played player resolves NO. A receiver's or passer's production also depends on the starting quarterback staying healthy. Lost games shift the whole remaining total down in game-sized steps. Loss of the starting job to benching, a QB competition or a portal arrival also ends a race without injury and is modelled separately from the injury hazard.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli per game with position-specific rates; season-ending injury is an absorbing state giving zero remaining production.

stages.name: Opportunity volume per game
stages.description: Volume is stat-specific: carries for rushing leaders (team rush attempts under expected script times carry share), targets for receivers (team dropbacks times target share), red-zone trips and pass share for passing touchdowns, and opponent dropbacks times pass-rush snaps for sacks. Stars on dominant teams lose fourth-quarter snaps in blowouts, while trailing teams pass more, which favours receivers on weaker teams.
stages.distribution: Team volume roughly normal per game; individual share is persistent but shifts with teammate injuries; sack opportunities scale with opponent pass rate.

stages.name: Conversion against remaining opponents
stages.description: Per-opportunity output (yards per carry, yards per target, touchdowns per scoring trip, sacks per pass-rush snap) is adjusted for the remaining opponents' run defense, coverage and pass protection, and for late-season weather in outdoor stadiums. Explosive-play rates matter because one 70-yard run can swing a close yards race.
stages.distribution: Heavy right tail for yards (explosive plays); passing TDs and sacks are small-count Poisson-like with overdispersion.

stages.name: Order statistic, ties and settlement
stages.description: End-of-regular-season totals for the full field (including unlisted contenders and teammates who split volume) are compared; the maximum wins, ties split $1/N rounded down, and official stat corrections or provider differences (half sacks, QB sack yardage counted as rushing) can change a close finish. The national series' 'Division I' wording leaves FCS inclusion open.
stages.distribution: Order statistic of correlated overdispersed totals; tie mass material for passing TDs and sacks.

contract_review.settlement_definition: YES if the named player records the most of the stated stat (passing TDs in the ACC, receiving yards in the Big 12, rushing yards in the Big Ten, sacks in the SEC, rushing yards in Division I) over the 2026 regular season. All regular-season games count including non-conference games; conference championship games are excluded (and so are bowls and CFP, which are postseason). If the player does not play in the conference (or in the regular season for the national series) for any reason, NO. Ties at the top pay YES $1/N rounded down to the cent, NO 1 minus that. The sampled text is truncated before the source-of-truth clause, so the stat provider is not visible.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official regular-season statistics; the sampled rules are truncated before the source clause, so whether Kalshi uses NCAA official stats, conference stats or a provider (ESPN) is unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: Stat type varies by series (passing TDs, receiving yards, rushing yards, sacks); each has a different volume driver and tie mass.
National series says 'Division I', which could include FCS players; conference series are limited to conference members.

Unequal game counts: teams with a Hawaii road game may play 13 regular-season games, teams with cancelled games fewer; conference title games excluded even though they are 'extra' games for top teams.
Player must 'play in' the conference; a player who plays zero snaps resolves NO, but partial seasons count normally.
College stat conventions: sacks count as rushing yards lost for QBs, sacks are recorded in half units; post-game stat corrections can change totals.
